analysis.one_liner: Removes Major League Baseball's special exemption from antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 1922 Supreme Court ruling, professional baseball has been the only major sport exempt from federal antitrust laws, letting team owners set league rules, control territories, and restrict player movement without facing competition lawsuits. This one-page bill would have removed that exemption, making baseball subject to the same antitrust laws as other businesses. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Baseball fans and players. Fans could benefit from more competition among teams and leagues, potentially affecting ticket prices and team locations, and players would gain the same antitrust rights against restraints on their salaries and mobility that other professional athletes have.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the special legal shield that protects Major League Baseball from competition law, letting players, rival leagues, and others sue over restraints like reserve rules and territorial monopolies.
It applies only going forward, so it changes the rules of competition without retroactively punishing past conduct.

analysis.who_pays: Major League Baseball team owners and the league, which would lose their exemption from antitrust suits and face potential challenges to league rules, territorial exclusivity, and player restraints.

drawbacks.text: Striping the exemption exposes club owners and leagues to lawsuits, damages, and uncertainty over routine league rules like drafts, revenue sharing, and territorial rights, which owners argued could destabilize the sport's business model.
The bill died without committee action, so no hearing ever weighed these trade-offs publicly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a one-page fix to a well-known anomaly with clear benefits for players and fans and modest costs confined to league rulemaking; the only real drawbacks are litigation uncertainty and the risk that full antitrust exposure prompts stricter league controls. Its main flaw was never getting a fair hearing: it died in committee without a markup or vote despite bipartisan sponsorship.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, dying when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 106 was introduced January 4, 1995 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
No further action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
The bill carried bipartisan cosponsorship from seven members, four Democrats and three Republicans, but that support was never tested on the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major League Baseball owners, who kept their antitrust exemption and the legal protection it provides for league rules, territorial rights, and player restraints.

for.name: Reps. Jacobs, Bunning, and Owens
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took it up, so the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors and cosponsors split evenly between the parties, 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and no floor vote ever tested broader support.

industries.industry: Major League Baseball club owners and league offices
industries.note: They would lose their exemption from antitrust law and become vulnerable to lawsuits over league rules, territorial monopolies, and player restraints. Fans and players could challenge practices that keep ticket prices up and player mobility down.
Players could sue over league practices that suppress their salaries and movement between teams, the same rights other professional athletes already had.
Rival baseball leagues could more easily challenge being shut out of cities and markets, though the bill's scope was limited to baseball.
